title.text: Words as numbers: bag of words, TF-IDF, embeddings and distance

objects.text: How can a computer find the right clause or policy when I describe it in plain words?

Applied AI and Automation  |  Session 4 of 14
KLAi Professional Learning  |  Jotham Martin Wambi

slides.notes:
Last time you measured a model with a confusion matrix and a threshold, and every example was a table of numbers. Most business data is words, and a computer only handles numbers. Today text becomes numbers too. We start with an everyday example, three friends rating two films, to meet vectors and four ways of measuring how close two of them are.

Then the same ideas apply to text: from a simple word count to the embeddings behind search by meaning. You work the measures out by hand.

slides.notes:
To answer that question, today has three parts. You will see how a message becomes a vector: first as word counts, then as TF-IDF weights, then as an embedding. You will work out four measures by hand with a pencil: Euclidean distance, Manhattan distance, the dot product and cosine similarity.

And you leave with a cheat sheet of the four. You will also decide where semantic search could help or hurt in your own work.

title.text:
Your two hours: from film ratings to a
search that understands a description

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_plan_11.90x3.95_b80ef97a.png
objects.alt: The two hours in parts, in minutes

objects.text: The search results are recorded in advance. You can ask me to run any description of yours live.

slides.notes:
Here is how we get there. We start with something everyone knows, three friends rating two films, and see that a list of numbers is a vector. We work out the four standard ways of measuring how close two vectors are: Euclidean distance, Manhattan distance, the dot product and cosine similarity.

Then we turn text into vectors, in three steps, from a simple word count to an embedding. I run a live semantic search where a plain description finds the formal clause, term or policy, on three kinds of text. After the break you work the four measures out by hand on paper.

We finish with your own descriptions, and where this helps or hurts in your work.

title.text: Three questions from last time

runs.text: 1.  Why can accuracy mislead when the thing you look for is rare?
2.  What do precision and recall each ask?
3.  What happens when you lower the threshold?

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/icon_question_2.80.png
objects.alt: Three questions

objects.text: Answer aloud first. Then we check together.

slides.notes:
Three quick questions from Session 3. Answer aloud first, and then we check together. It is a warm-up to bring last time back.

Question one. Why can accuracy mislead when the thing you look for is rare? Take a moment.

A good answer is this. A model that always predicts the majority class scores very high and catches nothing. In our run, always saying on time scored 90.8 percent. Ask for the baseline, precision and recall.

Question two. What do precision and recall each ask? Say it to yourself first.

A good answer is this. Precision: of the cases flagged, how many were real, TP divided by TP plus FP. Recall: of the real cases, how many were flagged, TP divided by TP plus FN.

Question three. What happens when you lower the threshold? Think about your own work as you answer.

A good answer is this. The model flags more cases. It catches more real ones (true positives) and also raises more false positives.

If an answer was missing, last session’s take-away sheet or workbook page has it. Now to today.

already have and what it feeds

title.text: Words we use today

Term frequency times inverse document frequency: a count in which rare terms weigh more than common ones.
A vector of numbers, produced by a trained model, that represents the meaning of a text.
Two ways to measure the gap between vectors. Smaller means closer.
Two ways to measure agreement between vectors. Bigger means closer.

slides.notes:
6 words for today. I give the plain meaning of each, and we use every one of them before the end of the session.

Vector. A list of numbers, such as Ana's two film ratings (3, 4). Each position is a dimension.

Bag of words. A message as a vector of word counts. The word order is lost.

TF-IDF. Term frequency times inverse document frequency: a count in which rare terms weigh more than common ones.

Embedding. A vector of numbers, produced by a trained model, that represents the meaning of a text.

Euclidean and Manhattan distance. Two ways to measure the gap between vectors. Smaller means closer.

Dot product and cosine similarity. Two ways to measure agreement between vectors. Bigger means closer.

Keep those words close. The first idea uses them straight away, so let us begin.

title.text:
A vector is a list of numbers: three
friends rate two films out of 10

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_t04_tastes_7.70x4.80.png
objects.alt: A vector is a list of numbers: three friends rate two films out of 10

objects.text: Ana, Ben and Chloe rate Film 1 (a comedy) and Film 2 (an action film).

runs.text: Ana is the vector (3, 4).
Each film is one dimension.
Ben rates higher but likes the same mix as Ana.
Who has a taste closest to Ana?

slides.notes:
We start with something everyone knows: film tastes. Three friends rate two films out of ten. Ana gives the comedy a three and the action film a four. Ben gives six and eight. Chloe gives four and three. Each person is now a list of two numbers, and a list of numbers is called a vector.

Each position in the list is a dimension, so these are two-dimensional vectors, and we can draw each as an arrow from zero on squared paper. The question is: who has a taste closest to Ana?

Ben rates everything higher, Chloe leans the other way. There is more than one sensible way to measure closeness, and today we learn four.

title.text:
Euclidean distance is the straight-line
gap between two vectors

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_t04_m_euclid_11.90x4.25.png
objects.alt: Euclidean distance is the straight-line gap between two vectors

objects.text: Ana and Ben rate two films out of 10. Gold: the worked answer.

slides.notes:
The first measure is the one a ruler gives you: the straight-line gap between the tips of two arrows. Its name is Euclidean distance, after the Greek geometer, and in industry you will hear L2 distance. The formula is on the slide. Say it aloud: d of a and b equals the square root of the sum of a i minus b i, all squared.

Here a1 and a2 are Ana's ratings of Film 1 and Film 2, and b1 and b2 are Ben's. Take the gap on each film, three and four. Square each gap, nine and sixteen, add them to get twenty-five, and take the square root, five. The same recipe works for a list of any length. Smaller means closer. Zero would mean identical tastes.

title.text: Manhattan distance adds the gaps along each axis

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_t04_m_manhattan_11.90x4.25.png
objects.alt: Manhattan distance adds the gaps along each axis

objects.text: Also called city-block distance. The red path walks the grid: 3 across, 4 up.

slides.notes:
The second measure adds the gaps instead of squaring them. It is called Manhattan distance, also city-block distance, and in industry L1 distance, because it is the length of a walk along a street grid with no shortcuts through buildings. As a memory aid, think of walking three blocks across and four blocks up.

Where the analogy breaks: the real formula works for any number of dimensions, however many streets that takes. In words: the sum of the absolute gaps. The vertical bars mean the size of the gap with the sign ignored. For Ana and Ben the gaps are three and four, so the total is seven.

The straight line was five, and the grid walk is seven. Smaller means closer.

title.text:
The dot product multiplies
matching ratings and adds them

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_t04_m_dot_11.90x4.25.png
objects.alt: The dot product multiplies matching ratings and adds them

objects.text: A bigger score means closer. Ben scores higher than Chloe, partly because Ben's arrow is long.

slides.notes:
The third measure asks how much two vectors agree, instead of how far apart they are. It is the dot product. Multiply the two Film 1 ratings together, multiply the two Film 2 ratings together, and add. Ana with Ben: three times six is eighteen, four times eight is thirty-two, total fifty.

Ana with Chloe: three times four is twelve, four times three is twelve, total twenty-four. The formula in words: the sum of a i times b i. The symbol a1 next to b1 means a one times b one. Industry also calls it the inner product. Here bigger means closer.

But look at a weakness. Ben rates everything high, so Ben's arrow is long, and long arrows pick up big scores just for being long.

title.text:
Cosine similarity compares only
the angle between two vectors

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_t04_m_cosine_11.90x4.25.png
objects.alt: Cosine similarity compares only the angle between two vectors

objects.text: Ben points exactly the same way as Ana. Chloe is 16 degrees away.

slides.notes:
The fourth measure fixes the length problem by looking only at the angle. Cosine similarity is the dot product divided by the two lengths multiplied together. The length of an arrow is the square root of its squared ratings added. Ana is the square root of nine plus sixteen, which is five.

Ben is ten, and Chloe is five. Ana with Ben: fifty divided by five times ten is one. No angle at all, same direction. Ana with Chloe: twenty-four divided by twenty-five is zero point nine six, sixteen degrees apart. One means the same direction, zero means a right angle.

Cosine ignores length, and for text that is usually what we want. Industry also uses cosine distance, which is one minus the cosine similarity.

title.text:
The four measures can pick different
winners, so know which one you use

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_t04_compare4_7.70x4.80.png
objects.alt: The four measures can pick different winners, so know which one you use

objects.text: Who is closer to Ana: Ben, the enthusiast, or Chloe?

runs.text: Euclidean and Manhattan pick Chloe.
Dot product and cosine pick Ben.
Cosine is widely used for text, because length says little about meaning.

slides.notes:
You now have four measures, so let me put all four on one question. Who is closer to Ana: Ben, whose arrow is long, or Chloe, whose arrow is short?

Euclidean distance says Chloe, one point four against five. Manhattan distance says Chloe, two against seven. The dot product says Ben, fifty against twenty-four, because Ben's arrow is long. Cosine similarity says Ben, one against zero point nine six, because Ben points exactly the same way as Ana.

They disagree, and none of them is wrong. They measure different things. For text, cosine is widely used, because the length of a passage tells you little about its meaning. When a vendor says similarity, ask which measure.

title.text:
A bag of words turns a message
into a vector of word counts

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_t04_bow_7.70x4.80.png
objects.alt: A bag of words turns a message into a vector of word counts

objects.text: Like counting ingredients in a recipe: two eggs, one cup of flour. Here we count words.

runs.text: Message B has "the" twice and "late" once.
Order is lost: "man bites dog" equals "dog bites man".
Problem: "the" counts like "invoice".

slides.notes:
Now the same idea for text. A customer message is a short text, such as an order or a complaint, and we want the machine to compare messages. The simplest way to give a message numbers is to count words, much as a recipe counts ingredients. Here are four short invented messages.

For each we count how often a few words appear. Message B has the word the twice and the word late once. Each message becomes a row of numbers, a vector with one dimension per word. This is called a bag of words, because the words are shaken into a bag and the order is lost.

It is crude but useful. It treats every word as equally important, and that is the problem the next step fixes.

title.text:
TF-IDF gives rare terms more weight,
because a rare term points to its message

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_t04_tfidf_11.90x4.25.png
objects.alt: TF-IDF gives rare terms more weight, because a rare term points to its message

objects.text: Recorded run, 6 Nov 2026: message M06 of 40 invented messages. Real: scikit-learn defaults.

slides.notes:
That equal treatment is the weakness. TF-IDF stands for term frequency times inverse document frequency. Term frequency, tf, is how often a term appears in the message. Document frequency, df, is how many of the forty messages contain it. A term in few messages says more about its message than a term found everywhere.

The simplified column, in gold, multiplies tf by forty divided by df: invoice appears twice and is in four messages, so two times ten is twenty. The recorded run used the scikit-learn default form. The idf is the natural log of forty-one over one plus df, plus one.

The weight is tf times idf, divided by the length of the message vector. For invoice: two times 3.10, divided by 18.54, is 0.335. Weighting still cannot see meaning.

title.text:
An embedding is a vector that places a text
so that similar meanings sit close together

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_t04_plane_7.70x4.80.png
objects.alt: An embedding is a vector that places a text so that similar meanings sit close together

objects.text: A toy with two dimensions: how much a word is about money, and about trucks.

runs.text: invoice (4, 1): mostly money.
lorry (1, 4): mostly trucks.
Close arrows mean close meaning.
Real embeddings have hundreds of dimensions.

slides.notes:
Weighting helps, but it still cannot see meaning. The words flood and force majeure share no words, yet they are close in meaning. An embedding fixes that. It is a vector, like Ana's ratings, but its numbers describe meaning. Here is a toy with two dimensions that I chose myself: how much a word is about money, and how much about trucks.

Invoice and receipt point to the right. Lorry and truck point upwards. Close arrows mean close meaning. This is a vector space, and we can measure closeness in it with the four measures. In a real embedding nobody names the dimensions. A trained model learns hundreds of them.

Who chooses those numbers, though?

title.text:
A network produces the vector, trained
so that similar meanings land close

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_t04_network_11.90x4.25.png
objects.alt: A network produces the vector, trained so that similar meanings land close

objects.text: Simplified. The model is all-MiniLM-L6-v2: text in, 384 numbers out.

slides.notes:
A fair question is who chooses the numbers. Nobody does by hand. A neural network reads the text and produces them, much like the digit network of Session 1, which read 64 numbers and produced 10 scores. Here the text goes in, and 384 numbers come out. It is trained on a very large set of examples, over a billion pairs of related sentences for this model, so that texts with similar meaning end up with similar vectors.

That is a simplified account, and the picture draws the network small. The result is the vector space from the last slide, with 384 dimensions instead of two. So the numbers are learned, not written by a person. Now let us look at some real ones.

title.text:
A real embedding has 384 numbers:
nobody reads them, we compare them

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_t04_numbers_11.90x4.25.png
objects.alt: A real embedding has 384 numbers: nobody reads them, we compare them

objects.text: Recorded run, 6 Nov 2026, model all-MiniLM-L6-v2. Gold: close in meaning.

slides.notes:
Two numbers is a toy, so here is a real embedding from a recorded run. I used the small open model you just saw, all-MiniLM-L6-v2, whose model card says it turns a sentence into a vector of three hundred and eighty-four numbers. Here are the first eight numbers for three texts.

The first is a plain question about heavy rain flooding the road. The second is the force majeure clause, which is about events beyond anyone's control. The third is the governing law clause. The model produced them. No person can read them. We only compare them, with a measure like the ones we just worked, here cosine similarity.

The question and the force majeure clause score zero point three six. The governing law clause scores zero point zero three.

title.text:
Demonstration: describe a clause in
plain words and find its formal name

objects.text: I will show

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_flow_7.30x3.90_ff7e641d.png
objects.alt: Demonstration: describe a clause in plain words and find its formal name

objects.text: Watch for

runs.text: The right term in the top three.
A keyword search that finds nothing.
Compare scores only within one search.

slides.notes:
All four measures work on any vectors, so let me use them on real text. I type a plain description, and the computer returns the formal clause, term or paragraph that matches. This is called semantic search. Four steps. I describe it in plain words. The model turns my description into three hundred and eighty-four numbers.

It compares those numbers with the numbers of ten passages, using cosine similarity. And it ranks them, showing the top three. Next to it I show a keyword search, which looks only for shared words. You choose the kind of text: contract clauses, finance terms or HR policy paragraphs.

Watch for the right answer in the top three, and for the keyword search finding nothing at all.

title.text:
Contract clauses: the right clause came
first for all four plain descriptions

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_t04_search_11.90x4.25_fb6098b1.png
objects.alt: Contract clauses: the right clause came first for all four plain descriptions

objects.text: Recorded run, 6 Nov 2026. Gold: the right clause. Scores: cosine similarity.

slides.notes:
What did you see? The right answer near the top, and a keyword search that found little or nothing. That is semantic search at work. Here are the recorded results for contract clauses. On the left, four descriptions in plain words. What happens if heavy rain floods the road and the delivery cannot get through?

The model puts force majeure first, at zero point three six. Who pays us back if the supplier mistake costs us money?

Indemnity, first. Can we walk away without giving a reason?

Termination for convenience. The contract keeps running every year unless we say something in time?

Automatic renewal. In the last column, a keyword search finds the right clause for three of the four, and for the flood question no clause shares a single word with the description.

title.text:
Finance terms: first once, in the top three
for three of four, so a person still chooses

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_t04_search_11.90x4.25_a24ea585.png
objects.alt: Finance terms: first once, in the top three for three of four, so a person still chooses

objects.text: Recorded run, 6 Nov 2026. The right term was fourth for the second description.

slides.notes:
Clean results like that can mislead, so here is the same run on finance and invoice terms. This one is messier, and I show it on purpose. For the money we owe the maize miller, the right term, accounts payable, came second behind depreciation. For three-way match, the right term came first.

For make sure our books match what the bank says, bank reconciliation came second, behind bad debt write-off. And for the shop that sent back damaged bags, the right term, credit note, came fourth, behind accounts receivable. That is a reasonable answer to the question, because the shop does owe us money. Semantic search gives a shortlist, and a person picks from it.

title.text:
HR policy: the right paragraph was in the top three
for all four, and keyword search found none first

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_t04_search_11.90x4.25_36806265.png
objects.alt: HR policy: the right paragraph was in the top three for all four, and keyword search found none first

objects.text: All 12 searches: right answer first 7, in the top three 11; keyword search first 4.

slides.notes:
That shortlist idea holds for the third kind of text, HR policy paragraphs. The person afraid to report a colleague who steals stock gets whistleblowing, first. The malaria message gets sick leave, first. The unhappy employee who wants to complain gets the disciplinary procedure first and the grievance procedure second.

The person who wants to quit gets the notice paragraph second. In all four the right paragraph is in the top three, and the keyword search never puts the right one first. Over all twelve searches: semantic search had the right answer first in seven and in the top three in eleven. Keyword search had it first in four.

title.text:
The four measures agree when vectors have
equal length, and part ways when they do not

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_t04_agree_7.70x4.80.png
objects.alt: The four measures agree when vectors have equal length, and part ways when they do not

objects.text: This model sets every vector to length 1 as a last step. Skip it and the measures split.

runs.text: Same question, lengths left alone: Euclidean distance says bank reconciliation.
Dot product and cosine say bad debt write-off.
No measure is right every time.

slides.notes:
All that ranking used cosine similarity, so you may ask whether another measure would change the winner. Mostly it would not, and here is why. By default this model scales every vector to exactly length one as its last step. With equal lengths, Euclidean distance, the dot product and cosine similarity always give the same order, and Manhattan distance usually.

In our twelve searches all four agreed on the top answer in eleven. I can skip that last step and leave the lengths alone. Then they split. For the question about matching our books to the bank, the two candidate vectors have lengths four point five and five point three.

Euclidean and Manhattan distance pick bank reconciliation, the right one. The dot product and cosine pick bad debt write-off. Check the top three, whichever measure you use.

title.text:
A 2D map of the embeddings shows the clusters,
but keeps only 18 percent of the information

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_t04_map_7.70x4.80.png
objects.alt: A 2D map of the embeddings shows the clusters, but keeps only 18 percent of the information

objects.text: Reduce 384 dimensions to 2 and similar texts still sit together.

runs.text: Three clusters: contracts, finance, HR.
A description can sit far from its answer on the map.
The method is PCA, principal component analysis.

slides.notes:
Everything so far has been vectors and tables, so can we see all this?

Not in three hundred and eighty-four dimensions, so we reduce them to two. This is a real map of the thirty passages and twelve descriptions from today. A method called PCA, principal component analysis, keeps the two directions in which the points differ most. Another method is t-SNE.

Contract clauses cluster at the top, finance terms on the right, HR paragraphs on the left. Price adjustment, a contract clause, sits near the finance terms, which makes sense. But look at what the map loses. It keeps only eighteen percent of the variation in the numbers, a rough measure of the information.

A description can sit far from its answer on the map, even though in the full vectors it is close. Use a map to see clusters, never to measure distances.

title.text:
Work out the four measures
by hand for three viewers

objects.text: 15 minutes
Hands-on, no computer
Fill in the table for the three pairs.

runs.text: Mark A, B and C on squared paper.
Euclidean: √(gap₁² + gap₂²).
Manhattan: |gap₁| + |gap₂|.
Dot product: a₁b₁ + a₂b₂.
Cosine: dot product ÷ (length × length).

slides.notes:
You have seen the ideas and the search, so it is your turn with a pencil. Take fifteen minutes. Three viewers rate Film 1 and Film 2 out of ten: A gives three and four, B gives three and one, C gives six and zero. On squared paper, mark the three points and draw an arrow from the origin to each.

For each pair, work out four numbers using the formulas on the sheet. For Euclidean distance, square each gap, add, take the square root. For Manhattan distance, add the sizes of the gaps. For the dot product, multiply matching ratings and add. For cosine, divide the dot product by the two lengths: A is five, B is three point one six, C is six.

When you have the twelve answers, ask which pair each measure calls closest. They will not all agree.

Predict whether a keyword search would find it, and whether a semantic search would. Write yes, no or unsure.
